cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31546.summary: A circular medallion with the busts of a couple – their faces left unfinished – divides two registers of biblical scenes in which Christ heals, multiplies the loaves and raises the dead. The blank faces show that such sarcophagi were carved in advance and personalised (or not) when bought.
facts: The Commons description notes the 'clipeo (busti non finiti)', the unfinished portrait busts.

cur:catacombs2-ny-carlsberg-jonah-good-s.summary: On this small sarcophagus for a child, the story of Jonah fills the front: sailors cast the prophet from a ship under full sail into the coils of the sea monster, while a wind-god blows from above, and at the right Jonah is cast up again amid a tangle of vegetation. At the left end stands a shepherd in a short tunic with a sheep on his shoulders, the Good Shepherd, a sign that the child is carried safely home by Christ.
facts: Jonah, swallowed and released after three days, was read by Early Christians as a sign of Christ's resurrection (Matthew 12:40), and was one of the most popular subjects of pre-Constantinian funerary art.
The museum label photographed on Commons dates it to around AD 300 and gives its origin as Rome.
cur:catacombs2-ny-carlsberg-jonah-good-s.notes: The inventory number IN 857 comes from the file name of Marie-Lan Nguyen's detail photograph; it was not checked against the museum's catalogue.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-jairus-daughter.summary: Before a walled building, Christ bends over the girl lying on a curtained couch and takes her hand, while her father Jairus, labelled 'senior', and apostles watch from the left.
facts: Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.
